Ibid. We should also note the bodily organs in the brain that Ibn Sīnā assigns to each of these powers of internal sensory perception. In Pointers and Reminders (vol. 2, pp. 353–355), he calls these bodily organs “instruments,” and sometimes refers to them as the “seat” of perception. In The Salvation, he simply gives the place “assigned” in the brain to each faculty. Common sense is “a faculty located in the first cavity of the brain”; the image-preserving faculty is “located at the back of the front cavity of the brain”; the imaginative faculty is “located in the middle cavity of the brain”; the estimative faculty is “located at the rear of the middle cavity of the brain”; and the retaining or memory faculty is “located in the rear cavity of the brain.” These locations naturally reflect the level of scientific knowledge of brain anatomy in the medieval Arab period. Philosophically, however, they also show an advanced tendency to connect the process of thought with the brain’s physical organs, which here points toward a materialist outlook. Modern science identifies the brain’s gray matter, especially the cerebral cortex, as one of the main physical organs involved in cognition.↩︎

We should quote the following passage because it clearly shows Ibn Sīnā’s method in his theory of universals. He says: “Universals, and the judgments and concepts that concern them, are not grasped by the senses or imagination, nor are they themselves objects of intuition or experience. But the senses and imagination assist the intellect. As for forming concepts: the senses present mixed things to the imagination, the imagination presents them to the intellect, and the intellect then separates, distinguishes, and divides them. It takes each meaning on its own and arranges what is more particular and more general, what belongs to the essence and what is accidental. In this way the first meanings needed for concepts become present in the intellect, and it then combines them into definitions. As for judgments, the senses and imagination may assist [the intellect] through experience or intuition, and they may assist it through induction.... They may also assist indirectly: first by helping to supply the concepts, after which the concepts are combined through affirmation and negation. The intellect then sees what must be accepted as self-evident, and it sees the syllogism by which other judgments must be acquired.” The Salvation, pp. 65–66. This passage gives a detailed account of how the intellect moves from sensory experience to the universal. It confirms that, in Ibn Sīnā’s theory of universals, the intellect depends on sensory experience. Intuition is mentioned here only incidentally. We will return to this later.↩︎

Modern scholars disagree about the intellectual relationship between Pointers and Reminders and Ibn Sīnā’s earlier works, especially The Healing and The Salvation. Some argue that when Ibn Sīnā wrote Pointers and Reminders, as well as his symbolic stories—The Treatise of the Bird, Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān, Salāmān and Absāl, and The Treatise on Love—he moved away from the Peripatetic ideas that stand out in The Healing and finally turned toward a Sufi form of illuminationist wisdom. This view is represented, for example, by L. Gardet in his article on the religious idea in Ibn Sīnā, published in Revue du Caire, June 1951, and by Sulaymān Dunyā in the introduction to his Cairo 1947 edition of Pointers and Reminders. Other scholars deny that The Healing and Ibn Sīnā’s other early works ceased to express his real views. This is the position of scholars such as Carra de Vaux, Avicenna, Arabic ed., p. 150, and the French Orientalist A. M. Goichon in The Philosophy of Ibn Sīnā, Arabic ed., Beirut, 1950, p. 18. We accept this second view. We have found nothing in Pointers and Reminders that Ibn Sīnā had not already said in his other works. The book differs mainly in two ways. The first is formal: the way it is composed, the material is arranged, and the discussion is divided into sections. The second concerns expression: the style used to present the ideas and the beauty of the language. The writing is more concentrated and compressed, and in the later chapters Ibn Sīnā sometimes uses symbols and sometimes interprets the outward wording of Qurʾānic passages. These stylistic features may be what idealist scholars used to support the claim that Ibn Sīnā changed the positions expressed in his earlier works, where some materialist tendencies are visible, and ended by adopting an illuminationist-Sufi outlook. Some of these scholars also appeal to remarks in the introduction to a work published under Ibn Sīnā’s name as The Logic of the Easterners (Cairo, 1910), where he appears to disagree with the Peripatetics. They also use Ibn Ṭufayl’s statement in the introduction to Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān that Ibn Sīnā said at the beginning of The Healing that the truth as he understood it was different from what that book contained. See Ibn Ṭufayl, Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān, Dār al-Maʿārif ed., Beirut, 1954, p. 8. In reality, even in The Healing, Ibn Sīnā does not agree completely with Aristotle or with Peripatetic philosophy in general. He differs from them on many points and alters many positions. As for the special section of Pointers and Reminders on the “Stations of the Knowers,” first, it is a mixture of ideas scattered through his other books; and second, it is a descriptive discussion, not a reflection of Ibn Sīnā’s own way of life, as we know from his historically well-established biography.↩︎

The Qurʾānic passage in question is: “God is the light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light is as a niche containing a lamp; the lamp is in a glass; the glass is like a shining star, lit from a blessed olive tree, neither eastern nor western, whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it—light upon light...” (Qurʾān 24:35). Ibn Sīnā applies this verse to the levels of intellect in his own theory. He interprets the “niche” as the material intellect; the “olive tree” as the thinking faculty—that is, rational reflection assisted by sensory perceptions; the “oil” as intuition, through which knowledge is gained without discursive thought; the “glass” as the habitual intellect; the phrase “whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it” as the highest degree of intuition, which he calls the holy faculty; and “light upon light” as the stage of perfection reached when the intellect becomes an acquired intellect. He interprets the “lamp” as the rational faculty once it becomes an actual intellect: the human soul can then “bring before itself, whenever it wishes, an intelligible already acquired and completed as though it were directly present, without needing to acquire it again” (Pointers and Reminders, vol. 2, pp. 369–376). Al-Ghazālī, however, reverses the relation and treats the Qurʾānic verse as an interpretation of these levels of theoretical intellect. See al-Ghazālī, The Niche of Lights, p. 58.↩︎

In logic, the middle term is the universal proposition relied on in a syllogism to move from what is known to what is unknown—that is, from the minor premise to the required conclusion. This universal proposition, which functions as the middle term, may come either from first rational principles, or axioms, or from theoretical propositions derived from the particulars of external reality. In both cases, even for Ibn Sīnā himself, it is a reflection of external reality, as we concluded earlier from his theory of how first principles are known.↩︎

The question of how consciousness arises in the brain remained unclear to scientists until the famous Soviet scientist Pavlov explained it in the way we described earlier. Before Marx, this question remained a puzzle even for materialist philosophers. Like the idealists, some materialists would say either that consciousness is an essence completely independent of matter, so that body and consciousness work separately but in parallel by some kind of miracle, or they would give a crude explanation and say that the brain secretes thought just as the mouth secretes saliva—that thought simply flows from it automatically. Lenin criticized this crude view, arguing that explaining thought as matter is just as false as explaining matter as thought, because vulgar materialism quickly slips into idealism.↩︎

Ibn Sīnā wrote a special chapter in The Salvation (p. 189) entitled “On the Unity of the Soul,” where he argues that the soul is a single entity in which all the faculties of the soul come together. From this he reaches an important conclusion: he acknowledges that the existence of the soul and the existence of the body are one. Yet he finally maintains that the soul does not arise from a body, “but from a substance whose substantiality is separate” (p. 192). This confirms what we have said: he saw the appearance of unity without seeing the underlying reality of that unity.↩︎
